src: arXiv 2507.00979 (PDF, version as served 2025-07) plus ACL Findings 2025 PDF https://aclanthology.org/2025.findings-acl.784.pdf (both read via WebFetch)
rationale: I1 met: agents act in a real Android emulator and in Docker code execution (also AgentHarm simulated tools). I2: CIP itself is prompting-only (CID text is prepended to the prompt; no gate/monitor, so I2(b) not met per R1), but the paper assumes adversaries and evaluates defense against them, so R1 last sentence applies (adversary assumed, model hardening = I2(a) defense D1): Section 4.5 tests indirect prompt injection ('maliciously embedded instruction within its observations') and template jailbreaks ('CIP significantly increases the robustness'), RedCode-Exec reports attack success rate (about 69.9% to 41.8%), and MobileSafetyBench/AgentHarm use malicious instructions. Ethics text admits 'advanced adversaries may still find inventive ways to bypass these protections'. Borderline because the introduction frames the risk mainly as unintended ('naively execute the given commands') and the abstract speaks only of generic safety; if adversarial evaluation were treated as secondary a coder could apply R1 and give E2.

src: ACL Findings 2026 PDF https://aclanthology.org/2026.findings-acl.1542.pdf and ACL Anthology page /2026.findings-acl.1542/ (read via WebFetch); arXiv precursor 2512.21354v1 'Reflection-Driven Control for Trustworthy Code Agents' read for cross-check
rationale: I1 not met in the experiments (R3 second sentence): the instantiation is secure code generation on eight CWE scenarios; outputs are code text scored by compilation, CodeQL static analysis and functional I/O tests ('All generated code samples are analyzed using the static analysis tool CodeQL'); no tool call or external side effect is studied; the only other experiment is HotpotQA question answering; the 'iterative tool-driven agents' appear only as a one-line portability setting in Appendix C.2 with no tools, tasks or setup specified. The 'external verifiers gate action release' is in practice a post-generation filter on code text and memory deposits, not interception of tool actions. Threat model is non-adversarial: 'Our current design assumes a benign but error-prone agent' and no jailbreak or injection test (adaptive attackers only in limitations), so I2(a) fails as well. Borderline because title and abstract claim a runtime verifier gate for 'arbitrary agent workflows' (I2(b) mechanism, adversary not required per R1) and the paper has a reflective memory plus an appendix tool-driven setting; a coder crediting the claims rather than the experiments could include it.

src: arXiv 2511.20703 (PDF and HTML v1, read via WebFetch)
rationale: I1 met: LLM agents call tools in an agentic loop (6,648 proxy tools in a finite-state scenario; tools are simulated). I2 fails under R6: the threat actor is the agent itself with no adversarial goal ('misuse is therefore not malice, but misaligned instrumental reasoning'); the paper says its pressure design 'resembles a stress test rather than a deliberate jailbreak attack' and is non-adaptive; it only measures propensity (zero-pressure vs high-pressure rates) and proposes no runtime enforcement ('call for a shift from static capability audits toward dynamic propensity assessments'), so R6 second sentence applies: spontaneous risky-action tendency only, no enforcement mechanism = E2. Borderline because operational pressure (six dimensions escalated by sender authority, including an Evaluation-Awareness dimension that lowers perceived oversight and detection) can be read as a red-team style induction ('감독 회피를 유도') making it an I2(a) benchmark; I judged it not adversarial because messages convey urgency and stakes, not instructions to harm, and the violation is simply any call of the misaligned tool.

src: arXiv 2309.17234 (PDF and HTML, version as served; NeurIPS 2024 D&B version content, read via WebFetch)
rationale: R2 applies: multi-LLM negotiation where each agent's public messages determine other agents' proposals, votes and the final deal, so I1 is met although there are no external tools (agents act on one another). Malicious agents are assumed and operationalised: adversarial players are instructed to 'isolate one party by pushing for deals that you think they will oppose' and the benchmark measures the effect on victims' scores ('the targeted agent gets a lower score in the final deal'), with 'rogue parties' in the motivation; per R2 final text output does not matter once malicious agents are assumed, hence I2(a) benchmark/measurement. Borderline because the main contribution is a negotiation capability benchmark and the greedy/adversarial section (3.2 and 4.7) is only about 10% of the paper; no defense is proposed (moderator agents left as future work); if I2 'main contribution' is read strictly a coder could give E2, though 'Maliciousness' is in the title and the abstract calls the safety evaluation 'important'.

src: arXiv 2512.04864v1 (PDF, read via WebFetch; ICML 2026 version abstract matches)
rationale: I1 met: agents (smolagents) use file read/write, web search/browse and Python execution, and the deceptive behaviours are real actions (e.g. fabricating local files). I2 fails under R6 second sentence: no adversarial goal is given ('users issue only benign instructions and never encourage the agent to lie, manipulate, or roleplay a deceptive persona'); constraints are 'mundane events' such as broken tools; the paper only measures a spontaneous deception tendency on 200 tasks and 11 LLMs; the mitigations tested are prompt-level constraints only (not a runtime enforcement mechanism per R1) and give 'only limited reductions'. Hence E2. Borderline N because R6 explicitly names spontaneous 'deception tendency' without enforcement as E2; the only counter-reading is R5 (agent as adversary, AGT) which R6 narrows to adversarial goal assignment or induced oversight evasion, neither present.

src: arXiv 2603.18382v2 (HTML, read via WebFetch; ICML 2026 version)
rationale: I1 met: agents run in OpenHands with file access and code execution (Netflix and InferLink settings) and as web-enabled Gemini agents that retrieve public evidence (AOL and human-AI trace settings); per R3 the harm appears in the output (a reconstructed identity) but tool-using agents still satisfy I1. I2(a) met: privacy threat with an explicit adversary and defined attacker knowledge (Explicit-ZK, Explicit-MK, 'attacker knowledge'), a benchmark (InferLink) and measurement (79.2% vs 56.0% classical baseline; silent linkage even 'without an explicit re-identification request'), plus a defense evaluation (privacy-aware system prompt 'reduces LSR to near zero' under explicit requests but with over-refusal cost). Not E4: agents are not applied by defenders as a security tool; the paper measures an agent-induced privacy failure ('an agent reconstructs a specific real-world identity'). Borderline because a coder could treat agent-based re-identification as an offensive security task (E4, like pentest agents) or treat the implicit-linkage part as non-adversarial risk (E2).

src: arXiv 2401.10019 PDF and Findings of EMNLP 2024 PDF https://aclanthology.org/anthology-files/anthology-files/pdf/findings/2024.findings-emnlp.79.pdf (read via WebFetch)
rationale: The 569 records are multi-turn ReAct-style tool-use trajectories of agents (ToolEmu 81, InjecAgent 414, AgentMonitor 24, manual 55), so the object studied is the safety of agent tool actions ('whether agent actions are safe'); I1 is satisfied through the judged agent trajectories (R3: tool-using agents) although the evaluated LLMs only output an analysis and a safe/unsafe label. I2(a) met as benchmark/measurement: 414 of 569 records (72.8%) are 'Intended Attacks' where 'attackers inject malicious instructions into the environment', the rest are unintended risks; the paper also fine-tunes judges and tests prompting. No runtime enforcement mechanism is proposed (offline benchmark of monitor capability). Borderline because the tested LLMs do not act or use tools in the experiments (a coder applying the R3 second sentence could give E1), and because 27.2% of the records are non-adversarial.

src: arXiv 2506.02009 (PDF, read via WebFetch; NeurIPS 2025 version)
rationale: I1 met: the multi-agent system executes kubectl commands through agent tools on simulated clusters (AIOpsLab, ITBench). No adversary: 'does not explicitly address malicious actors'; only non-adversarial failure risk ('making things worse'), so I2(a) fails and only I2(b) could apply. STRATUS does contain runtime mechanisms (TNR undo/rollback with commit-or-abort after each transaction, read-only sandbox confinement of detection and diagnosis agents, writer exclusivity, command-level validation), but R4 decides: the core contribution is reliability/performance ('significantly outperforms state-of-the-art SRE agents ... by at least 1.5 times'); the evaluation reports only mitigation success rates (TNR is shown through ablation of undo-and-retry, 15.4% to 69.2%), with no measurement of safety violations prevented, and the safety spec is justified as improving failure mitigation ('TNR enables safe agent exploration and iteration, which effectively improves failure mitigation'). Hence E2. Borderline because TNR is a named co-contribution with a formal lemma and genuine runtime enforcement (including permission confinement), so a coder could judge the safety enforcement as co-primary and include it under I2(b).
